A few years ago I was seriously looking into starting an ISP. I learned a lot during the course of my research, but I have pretty much given up because there is no practical way for me to get enough money to cover the startup costs. However, I feel that I am very knowledgeable about Net Neutrality and how important it really is.

Imagine if roads were owned by companies instead of governments. It seems reasonable that since they own the roads, they make the rules on their own property. But say the owner of the main road in your town owns a logging company. If you also own a logging company, they could charge you more or ban you from their roads. That leaves you with the options of paying more, or building another road along the same route as the other one. A second road would be prohibitively expensive for a small business, or stupid, redundant, and wasteful for a large one.

Net Neutrality means that the owner can't discriminate against competitive traffic. Being a Title II utility means that companies actually have to share their resources. Mobile phones are in this category, which is why you see small carriers renting or adding antennas on the towers of large carriers. Could you imagine if each cell site had several towers instead of just one? It would be ridiculous. Likewise, if I were to start an ISP, I could rent space on the poles that are already there instead of building another line parallel to the existing ones. This lowers costs, increases competition, and reduces inefficiencies.

Yes, it's giving the government more power, something I am generally against. But utilities are not like regular businesses. The internet only works because all the NETworks are INTERconnected. In order to sell you internet access, I have to connect to all the other ISPs in the world, and that isn't cheap. By requiring cooperation and lowering capital costs, it creates a healthy market for the consumer. The "capitalist" option of less regulation makes it easy for ISPs to form giant monopolies to stifle competition. The reason capitalism works is not because the government takes a laissez-faire approach to regulation. It works when there is a lot of competition. Hands off regulating is often the way to do that, but not this time.

The only 'problem' with capitalism is that if you take a full laissez-faire approach, you will end up with monopolies in each field and then you'll eventually end up with just one conglomerate running every business everywhere which leaves you with a dictatorship.
